extracted.intended_audience: Isabelle/Isar users, proof-tool developers, and researchers in interactive theorem proving
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and implementing automated proof procedures for Isabelle/Isar using the Eisbach proof method language; includes abstraction over terms, facts and methods, matching, combinators, and integration with Isabelle/ML. Targeted at making proof automation more accessible, maintainable, and readable within Isabelle developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design principle: easy to use for beginners and experts
rubrics_metrics.description: To be easy to use for beginners and experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eisbach aims to be accessible to existing Isar users so that a wider class of users can maintain and extend domain-specific proof procedures rather than requiring ML expertise. Examples: method-definition uses familiar Isar syntax; small ML snippets are available when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design principle: expose limited functionality, leave complex functionality to Isabelle/ML
rubrics_metrics.description: To expose limited functionality, leaving complex functionality to Isabelle/ML.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eisbach intentionally provides a high-level, untyped language for common proof procedures while allowing sophisticated features and optimizations to be implemented in Isabelle/ML. This design reduces surface complexity while retaining extensibility via ML (e.g., custom attributes, indexing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design principle: seamless integration with other Isabelle languages
rubrics_metrics.description: Seamless integration with other Isabelle languages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eisbach must interoperate with Isar syntax, Isabelle/ML, and object-logics (Isabelle/HOL). Implementation uses Isabelle's parsing framework to embed Isar tokens and attributes so Eisbach methods can invoke existing methods and attributes transparently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design principle: readable proof procedures (Isar principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: To continue Isar’s principle of readable proofs, creating readable proof procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method definitions should produce structured, human-readable proof procedures (instead of opaque scripts), maintaining the document-oriented Isar style and easing maintenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method-definition support (naming, combining, abstracting methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: The new Isar command method-definition allows proof methods to be combined, named, and abstracted over terms, facts and other methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'method-definition induct-list facts simp = (match ?concl in ?P (?x :: a list) ⇒ (induct ?x → fastforce simp: simp))' — after definition, the method can be invoked like any other Isar method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstraction over parameters (facts, terms, methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods may abstract over parameters: terms, facts, or other methods (via facts, for, and methods keywords).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fact parameters are supplied as lists (intro:, elim: etc.), term parameters via for with optional type constraints, and method-parameters via methods. This supports reusable, parameterized automation (examples: prop-solver2, elim-all).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact collections and declare-attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Support for creating and using named fact collections via declare-attributes and managing them in the proof context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: declare-attributes allows creation of new collections which methods can reference by [intro] etc.; facts can be augmented in the context or passed at invocation. Example: declare impI [intro] and conjE [elim] then use prop-solver3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinators and backtracking semantics (',', '|', '?', '+')
rubrics_metrics.description: Isar provides four combinators: ',' sequential composition with implicit backtracking, '|' alternative composition, '?' suppress failure (return original state), and '+' repeated application until failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the end of an apply command the first successful result is retained. Examples: '(rule impI, (erule conjE)?) | assumption)+' proves many propositional tautologies. The semantics of ',' produce all results of meth1 followed by meth2; first-success retention influences control flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custom combinator '→' that applies second method to all produced subgoals
rubrics_metrics.description: A fifth combinator ('→') invokes the second method on all subgoals produced by the first, unlike ',' which sequences with unknown subgoal counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Needed for cases where the number of subgoals cannot be known statically. Example: 'intro conjI → rule TrueI'. Used to define higher-order combinators like solve that check that a method discharges all produced subgoals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher-order methods / method parameters and combinators
rubrics_metrics.description: Support for higher-order methods that take other methods as parameters (methods keyword) and can apply them over produced subgoals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enables writing control combinators such as 'solve methods m = (m → fail)' or 'repeat-new methods meth = (meth → (repeat-new meth)?)'. These enable expressing policies like 'ensure this subcall solves all subgoals'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solve idiom: require a method to completely discharge its subgoals
rubrics_metrics.description: A higher-order pattern where a method is applied and then failure is triggered if any produced subgoals remain (e.g., solve m = (m → fail)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful to ensure recursive calls or guesses do not leave unsolved obligations; used in prop-solver and fol-solver to force full discharge or backtrack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching construct and its semantics (match against ?concl / prems / facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: An expressive match construct allows matching terms or fact collections against patterns with pattern-method pairs; ?concl and prems are special for the current subgoal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matching binds schematic variables and optionally names matched facts; successful matches serve as cut points for backtracking—once a pattern matches, subsequent patterns are not tried (contrast to Ltac). All possible unifiers for a matched pattern are explored. Examples: solve-ex, match-rules, guess-all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit subgoal focusing triggered by mentioning ?concl or prems
rubrics_metrics.description: Mentioning ?concl or prems causes implicit subgoal focusing, lifting goal parameters into fixed variables and premises into local assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focusing creates a uniform local context to enable matching and parameter passing inside method bodies; it preserves the ability of methods like erule to remove premises from the goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Static closure of concrete syntax (embedding token lists via parsing framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eisbach embeds most Isar syntax as uninterpreted token lists using Isabelle’s parsing framework that assigns values to tokens during parsing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoids re-implementing the parsers of many proof tools and attributes; at method application time Eisbach instantiates token values based on supplied arguments or match results and then executes the method body. Implementation detail but a design constraint to maintain Isar compatibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to include small Isabelle/ML snippets
rubrics_metrics.description: Small snippets of ML may be included on demand within Eisbach methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides escape hatches for functionality that Eisbach intentionally omits, enabling users to access the full power of ML for complex cases without making ML the default authoring mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility and forward/backward compatibility with Isar and existing methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Eisbach aims for seamless integration and compatibility with existing Isabelle proof methods and concepts (fact collections, attributes, tactics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design choices (untyped methods, embedding Isar tokens) were made to allow Eisbach to invoke existing methods and to be included in future Isabelle releases without breaking existing developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance and efficiency considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Eisbach implementations can have performance overhead; evaluation measured running time and identified hotspots (e.g., rule resolution costs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation: re-implementing two seL4 methods increased total proof running time from 8 minutes to 19 minutes for the benchmark; about 100 lines of ML were needed for compatibility and ~0.5% proof text changes. Guidance: possible optimizations include indexing facts and improving rule resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintainability: reduce duplication and lower maintenance costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary goal is to make writing proofs more productive, avoid duplication, and thereby lower the costs of proof maintenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By expressing automation at a high level and using readable method-definitions, Eisbach allows non-ML users to maintain domain-specific proof procedures; example: re-implementations of wp/wpc reduced ML code and made intent clearer, albeit with some efficiency trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressiveness: higher-order matching, recursion and solver construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Eisbach must support higher-order matching, recursion, and composition to express non-trivial solvers (e.g., propositional and first-order solvers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: prop-solver, guess-all, guess-ex, fol-solver combine matching, backtracking, and recursion to solve many standard logical problems. Matching considers only matches that bind all pattern variables to avoid trivial matches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching/backtracking semantic choice (cutpoint behavior vs Ltac)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eisbach chooses match semantics where a successful pattern match is a cut point: subsequent patterns are not attempted even if the inner method fails; all unifiers of the matched pattern are explored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This choice aligns with Isabelle's pervasive backtracking and the combinator semantics where inner failure should signal outer combinators; to emulate Ltac semantics one can use '?' and '|' to try subsequent patterns after failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debugging and traceability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Need for debugging features beyond manual printing of intermediate goal states; traces of matches and method applications with interaction are planned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: Eisbach currently lacks advanced debugging; planned features include interactive traces that show match results and method applications to aid development of complex methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for structured language elements and explicit subgoal addressing
rubrics_metrics.description: Desire to add more structured language elements (e.g., explicit subgoal production and addressing) for more natural integration with Isar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These features would make it easier to control goal decomposition and goal addressing, complementing existing combinators and implicit focusing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallel evaluation support for method combinators
rubrics_metrics.description: Eisbach should support parallel evaluation by default where combinator structure permits; e.g., (→) could use parallel THEN_ALL_NEW.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parallel skeletons could map naturally to method combinators to improve performance (analogy to PARALLEL_GOALS tactical in Isabelle/ML); this is a planned enhancement to improve scalability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typed vs untyped design tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Eisbach is deliberately untyped, resembling Ltac, to interoperate with untyped Isar proof methods; typed tactic languages (like Mtac) avoid dynamic errors but are harder to interoperate with untyped infrastructure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While typed method contracts are attractive, Eisbach opts for untyped methods to call existing methods; higher-order methods can approximate runtime contracts and arbitrary contract languages could be layered on top later.
